generation.hypothesis: In a low‐Al high-entropy alloy (specifically Al0.1CrCoFeNi), systematic variation of temperature will trigger a microstructural transition (from a clustered, disordered state toward a more ordered state) that moderates dislocation dynamics and hence plastic deformation behavior.
generation.material_initial_state: Al0.1CrCoFeNi high-entropy alloy in a predominantly disordered FCC state with weak clustering prior to deformation.
generation.intervention: Application of in-situ high-temperature tensile testing with digital image correlation and EBSD while systematically varying the temperature from cryogenic to high-temperature conditions under quasi-static loading.
generation.conditions: Tests performed over a wide temperature range (spanning cryogenic to elevated temperatures, e.g., up to 900 °C) under controlled strain rate and loading conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Temperature-induced alterations in microstructure, namely a clustering-to-ordering transition and changes in dislocation arrangement and mobility.
generation.mechanism: Increasing temperature activates atomic rearrangement in the alloy, reducing the extent of clustering and facilitating reordering. This transition modulates dislocation movement—initially hindering deformation at lower temperatures but enhancing ductility and altering flow stress at higher temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: At lower temperatures, the alloy will display relatively high yield strength and limited plasticity due to pronounced clustering. At higher temperatures, the transition toward a more ordered microstructure will facilitate dislocation motion, resulting in lower yield strength paired with increased ductility.
generation.baseline: The deformation behavior observed at ambient temperature, where the microstructure remains largely disordered and clustering is dominant.
generation.boundary: This temperature-dependent behavior is expected primarily in low-Al-content CrCoFeNi high-entropy alloys and may not extend to HEAs with significantly different compositions or to single-element systems.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative relationship between temperature and the extent of the clustering-to-ordering transition—and its precise effects on yield strength and ductility—requires further experimental validation. Additionally, the possible roles of twinning and other phase transformations under specific temperature ranges remain to be fully elucidated.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare Al0.1CrCoFeNi samples and conduct a series of tensile tests across a range of temperatures (e.g., cryogenic, room temperature, and high temperature) using in-situ digital image correlation and EBSD. Quantitatively map the microstructural evolution (e.g., clustering-to-ordering transformation) and measure mechanical properties (yield strength, ductility, dislocation density).
measurements: Yield stress and strain-to-failure at each temperature
EBSD microstructural maps indicating the degree of ordering
Digital image correlation data to capture strain localization
Dislocation density and analysis from micrographs
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If there is no significant microstructural transition (absence of clustering-to-ordering change) or if the measured mechanical properties do not exhibit the predicted temperature-dependent trends (i.e., consistent yield strength and ductility across the temperature range), the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Computational investigations of structural, chemical, and deformation behavior in high-entropy alloys (HEAs), which possess notable mechanical strength, have been limited due to the absence of applicable force fields. To extend investigations, we propose a set of intermolecular potential parameters for a quinary Al-Cr-Co-Fe-Ni alloy, using the available ternary Embedded Atom Method and Lennard-Jones potential in classical molecular-dynamics simulations. The simulation results are validated by a comparison to first-principles Korringa-Kohn-Rostoker (KKR) - Coherent Potential Approximation (CPA) [KKR-CPA] calculations for the HEA structural properties (lattice constants and bulk moduli), relative stability, pair probabilities, and high-temperature short-range ordering. The simulation (MD)-derived properties are in quantitative agreement with KKR-CPA calculations (first-principles) and experiments. We study Al x CrCoFeNi for Al ranging from 0 ≤ x ≤2 mole fractions, and find that the HEA shows large chemical clustering over a wide temperature range for x < 0.5. Abstract High entropy or compositionally complex alloys provide opportunities for optimization towards new high-temperature materials. Improvements in the equiatomic alloy Al 17 Co 17 Cr 17 Cu 17 Fe 17 Ni 17 (at.%) led to the base alloy for this work with the chemical composition Al 10 Co 25 Cr 8 Fe 15 Ni 36 Ti 6 (at.%). Characterization of the beneficial particle-strengthened microstructure by scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and observation of good mechanical properties at elevated temperatures arose the need of accomplishing further optimization steps. For this purpose, the refractory metals hafnium and molybdenum were added in small amounts (0.5 and 1.0 at.% respectively) because of their well-known positive effects on mechanical properties of Ni-based superalloys. By correlation of microstructural examinations using SEM with tensile tests in the temperature range of room temperature up to 900 °C, conclusions could be drawn for further optimization steps. Keywords: HEA, high entropy alloys, compositionally complex alloys, mechanical characterization
